quorum.judges_note: THE BINDING JUDGES ON THIS CUT ARE NOT THE LANES. Three of the four refutations came from instruments that ruled before any lane saw the branch: gate H refused the crux rows (backticks inside the key span it greps), the commit-msg hook refused a cut commit whose ticket said completed, and reading README.md refuted the receipt's claim that its version lines were already correct. The fourth came from lane 1. judges=3 counts the three lanes asked per round, across three rounds, of which a verdict came back from two at most; it is not three independent tiers and must not be read as such. .quorum/evidence/release-1.31.0-judges.md names each refuting authority.

Both now say 1.31. Gate D passed either way, because Cargo reads 1.30 as >=1.30.0, <2.0.0, which is why nothing else would have caught it.

R2: 'the cut's own ticket can be marked completed in the cut's own PR' — refused by the commit-msg hook: 'Pmat-Ticket PMAT-574 is completed — work belongs to an open item, and CB-2113 refuses this commit in CI'. PMAT-574 stays inprogress; the booking PR closes it.

R4: 'the receipt's diff list is complete' — lane 1, cited: it named the dogfood receipt and the cut log but not the receipt doing the listing, nor the quorum artifacts.

R5: 'the 42-vs-43 difference in CB-2115 is the receipts this commit had not yet added' — written into both the cut log and the dogfood receipt, refuted by round 3's lane 1: a markdown file cannot move ORPHAN-ROADMAP, ORPHAN-GITHUB or DRIFT. crux.verdict: docs/audits/crux-1.31.0.md, three rows, one per behaviour bullet, each naming >= 3 of the 28 surveyed systems. Written by the release orchestrator from documentation memory rather than surveyed by an agy lane as 1.29.0's was, every third-party claim marked [X], and the audit's Method section says so in its first paragraph. It also states what is NOT reconciled: PMAT-565 was still open at the cut, so its behaviour owes no row.
systems: Bazel, Ansible, Terraform, Kubernetes: a selection that matches nothing is an error in Bazel and in modern Ansible's --limit, while kubectl prints 'No resources found' and exits 0 [X] — forjar had the kubectl shape, and worse, because its empty selection still graded two resources from another manifest

systemd, Ansible, Puppet, Chef, Podman: systemd distinguishes the unit file on disk from the unit it has loaded [X]; the configuration managers all converge on state/enabled and manage the unit FILE separately [X]; the container world identifies what runs by DIGEST [X], which is what exec_sha256 is

Terraform, Puppet, Kubernetes, Ansible: -detailed-exitcode (2), --detailed-exitcodes (2) and kubectl diff (1) all put a difference in the exit code [X], while ansible --check exits 0 and makes you parse the recap [X] — forjar's verdict was real but flag-gated, which is an un-gated bug for every caller that did not know the flag
